poiKIM-desc:
The Kimpwanza League takes its name from the Lumbu ya kimpwanza, the Day of Freedom, as the Congolese call {{poiKIM002|the breakup of the old African Union}}. Led from Kinshasa by the Union of the Kongo, it joins Angola and South Africa into a bloc that spans the south-west of the continent, from {{poiKIM004|the Atlantic coast}} to the Cape.

Its founding idea is freedom as {{poiKIM001|Andre Ilunga}} defines it: not the freedom to fight whoever you like, but the freedom to feel safe living however you choose, guarded by the police cameras that make it possible. Its critics in the east call the same thing anarchistic nativism.

The League sits on some of the richest ground on Earth: the cobalt and copper of the Kongo, the chromium, manganese, titanium and coal of South Africa, and Angola's oil. It distrusts corporations, and waves off their diplomacy, yet much of its cobalt still finds its way through the brokers of Morgan Industries. Its great rival is the East African Federation, which dreams of a single Pan-African nation and regards the League as the wound that broke the last one. The two have watched each other across {{poiKIM003|the Mwitanzige Rift}} for decades.
poiKIM001-desc:
The dissolution of the African Union was a bloody and confusing affair, known by many names. The Congolese call it Lumbu ya kimpwanza, the Day of Freedom. The East Africans call it the Talaka, the Divorce. Andre Ilunga, leader of the Union of the Kongo and the heart of the Kimpwanza League, calls it a godsend.

He was born in 2151, the year independent Congo was founded, and watched every man and woman in his city join the militias. They were not fighting the African Union but the new Congolese state, for a state of their own for the Luba people. The nationalist fire of the Day of Freedom could not be put out. Ilunga moved to the megacity of Kinshasa, studied history and political science, and slowly lost faith in his kin's idea of freedom. Freedom, he decided, is not the freedom to fight whoever you like. It is the ability to feel safe doing whatever you want: to practise any faith, speak any language and change yourself in any way possible.

He became Mayor of Kinshasa in 2180 and Ntuadusi of the Kongo in 2185, and set out to build a land of freedom. Men and women walk its streets with their augments on display, a cross around their neck and a police camera watching their every move. What is freedom, if not feeling safe from those who would take it away? Ilunga knows the Federation would happily take it away at any moment.
poiKIM002-desc:
The breakup of the African Union began with the Congo Crisis of 2134: a nativist uprising in the Congo region that crippled the Union with armed conflict and political upheaval, cut it off from West Africa and finally tore it apart.

Both sides still live in its shadow. Many African Union units were stranded in West Africa when the crisis cut them off, and the East African Federation has governed under emergency powers enacted during the crisis ever since, justified as a shield against the populism and nativism that broke the Union. For the League, the crisis was the birth of its freedom. For the Federation, it is the catastrophe it has sworn never to let happen again.
poiKIM003-desc:
The Mwitanzige Rift runs along the border between the Kongo and the East African Federation, around its namesake lake. For decades it has been held by local warlords, too entrenched to remove and too useful to oppose, and it serves both powers as a buffer.

The buffer is wearing thin. The warlords fight among themselves, conditions in the Rift deteriorate, and the Kongo has begun reaching out to them with overtures. Kinshasa has also noticed that the warlords who raid its side of the border carry modern weapons of East African origin. Congolese officials accuse the Federation of backing them. The Federation denies it, and has offered no explanation of where the weapons came from.
poiKIM004-desc:
The League keeps its eyes on the east. Its armies, fortifications and politics are built around the East African Federation, and its long Atlantic coast has been left under-defended as a result.

Others have noticed. Biafra, across the Gulf of Guinea, sees the League's west coast as an opportunity, and Morgan Industries has its own ideas about the future of southern Africa. The League's anti-corporate instincts have kept Morgan's diplomacy at arm's length so far. Whether they can keep out Morgan Security is another question.
